primary_meaning: “Hate” is most commonly understood not as a fixed biblical symbol but as hostility, rejection, or settled opposition—the moral contrary of love. In Christian teaching, hatred of other people ordinarily signifies sinful alienation from God and neighbor.
primary_basis: Leviticus 19:17–18 — hatred of one’s brother is prohibited alongside the command to love one’s neighbor.
Matthew 5:43–44 — Jesus contrasts hating enemies with loving and praying for them.
1 John 2:9–11 — hatred of a brother is associated with darkness and spiritual blindness.
1 John 3:15 — hatred of a brother is equated morally with murder.
1 John 4:20 — professed love for God is incompatible with hatred of one’s brother.
Galatians 5:19–23 — hatred or enmity belongs to the works of the flesh, contrary to the fruit of the Spirit.

alternatives.meaning: In some biblical idioms, especially comparisons involving loyalty or preference, “hate” means “love less,” subordinate, or reject in favor of another rather than feel emotional hostility.
basis: Genesis 29:30–33 — Leah is described as “hated” in contrast with Jacob’s greater love for Rachel.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 — the “loved” and “hated” wives form a preference contrast.
Luke 14:26 — hating one’s family and life is commonly read as radical subordination of all other loyalties to Christ.
Matthew 10:37 — the parallel teaching is expressed as loving family more than Jesus.

alternatives.meaning: Hatred can denote righteous moral abhorrence of evil rather than malice toward persons.
basis: Psalm 97:10 — those who love the Lord are commanded to hate evil.
Proverbs 8:13 — fear of the Lord is identified with hatred of evil, pride, and corrupt speech.
Amos 5:15 — Israel is commanded to hate evil and love good.
Romans 12:9 — believers are told to abhor evil and cling to what is good.
Revelation 2:6 — hatred of the Nicolaitans’ works is commended.

alternatives.meaning: When attributed to God, “hate” is read as divine rejection, judicial opposition, or covenantal non-election; interpreters differ over whether it also describes a form of personal divine abhorrence.
basis: Malachi 1:2–3 — “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
Romans 9:10–13 — Paul cites the Jacob–Esau contrast in discussing election.
Psalm 5:4–6 — God is said to hate evildoers.
Psalm 11:5 — God’s soul is said to hate the wicked and the lover of violence.
Hosea 9:15 — divine hatred appears in a context of covenant judgment.

alternatives.meaning: Hatred may represent the world’s opposition to Christ and his disciples, expressing estrangement from God and resistance to divine revelation.
basis: John 3:19–20 — those who do evil hate the light.
John 7:7 — the world hates Jesus because he testifies against its works.
John 15:18–25 — the world’s hatred of disciples continues its hatred of Christ and the Father.
1 John 3:13 — believers should not be surprised if the world hates them.

notes: There is broad agreement about the ordinary moral sense of hatred and about several context-specific uses, but “hate” has no single settled symbolic meaning across Scripture. Its force depends on context: personal hostility, comparative preference, covenantal rejection, divine judgment, moral abhorrence of evil, or opposition to Christ.
